name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
summary: First great Olmec capital and earliest monumental centre in Mesoamerica, source of the colossal stone heads.

name: La Venta
summary: Olmec ceremonial city with the earliest large clay pyramid in Mesoamerica and buried serpentine offerings.

name: Tres Zapotes
summary: Late Olmec and Epi-Olmec centre; Stela C carries one of the earliest Long Count dates known.

name: Laguna de los Cerros
summary: Olmec centre controlling basalt quarries of the Tuxtlas that supplied monumental sculpture elsewhere.

name: Chalcatzingo
summary: Highland trade town whose Olmec-style cliff reliefs show interregional elite culture far from the Gulf coast.

name: Cuicuilco
summary: First city of the Basin of Mexico, with a great circular pyramid, buried by the Xitle lava flow.

name: Tlatilco
summary: Large Preclassic village-town in the Basin of Mexico known for its figurines and rich burials.

name: Teotihuacan
summary: Largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas, grid-planned around the Avenue of the Dead, with vast apartment compounds.

name: Cholula
summary: Continuously occupied pilgrimage city holding the largest pyramid by volume on Earth, the Tlachihualtepetl.

name: Monte Albán
summary: Zapotec capital built on a levelled mountaintop, with early writing and conquest-slab records.

name: Mitla
summary: Zapotec religious capital and burial place of high priests, famed for geometric stone mosaic facades.

name: Yagul
summary: Fortified Postclassic Zapotec town with palace complex and one of Mesoamerica's largest ballcourts.

name: Dainzú
summary: Zapotec valley town whose carved slabs depict helmeted ballplayers in an early distinctive style.

name: El Tajín
summary: Classic Veracruz capital with the niched Pyramid and seventeen ballcourts, centre of a ballgame cult.

name: Xochicalco
summary: Fortified Epiclassic hilltop city that rose after Teotihuacan, with an observatory cave and calendar reform stelae.

name: Cacaxtla
summary: Epiclassic hilltop citadel whose battle murals fuse highland and Maya painting traditions.

name: Teotenango
summary: Walled Matlatzinca hill city of the Toluca valley, abandoned soon after the Spanish conquest.

name: Tula
summary: Toltec capital whose Atlantean warrior columns and legend of Tollan shaped later Aztec political claims.

name: Tenayuca
summary: First Chichimec capital in the Basin of Mexico, with a serpent-ringed twin-stair pyramid prototype.

name: Azcapotzalco
summary: Tepanec imperial capital that dominated the Basin of Mexico until the Aztec Triple Alliance destroyed it in 1428.

name: Tenochtitlan
contested: Founding of 1325 CE is a traditional Mexica date recorded in later codices.
summary: Aztec island capital of causeways and chinampas, one of the world's largest cities in 1519.

name: Tlatelolco
contested: Traditional founding date from Mexica annals.
summary: Twin city of Tenochtitlan and site of the greatest market in the Americas, absorbed by conquest in 1473.

name: Texcoco
summary: Acolhua capital and intellectual centre of the Triple Alliance under the poet-king Nezahualcoyotl.

name: Tlacopan
summary: Third and junior partner of the Aztec Triple Alliance, successor to Tepanec power west of the lake.

name: Malinalco
summary: Aztec ritual town with temples cut directly into living rock for eagle and jaguar warrior orders.

name: Tzintzuntzan
summary: Capital of the Purépecha (Tarascan) empire, with five round yácata platforms above Lake Pátzcuaro.

name: Ihuatzio
summary: Earlier Purépecha capital of the Pátzcuaro basin, with walled causeways and yácata pyramids.

name: Pátzcuaro
summary: Founding seat of Purépecha kingship and later the first colonial capital of Michoacán.

name: Cempoala
summary: Totonac capital and the first large city Cortés entered, whose ruler allied against the Aztecs.

name: Quiahuiztlán
summary: Totonac cliff town above the Gulf with a hillside cemetery of miniature temple tombs.

name: Nakbé
summary: Earliest large Maya centre, with monumental triadic architecture centuries before the Classic period.

name: El Mirador
summary: Preclassic Maya megacity whose La Danta complex is among the largest structures ever built, linked by causeways.

name: Uaxactún
summary: Maya city with the earliest known astronomical E-Group, conquered by Teotihuacan-backed Tikal in 378.

name: Tikal
summary: Dominant Classic Maya kingdom of temple-pyramids and reservoirs, rival of Calakmul for lowland supremacy.

name: Calakmul
summary: Seat of the Snake Kingdom that built the largest Maya hegemony through vassal alliances against Tikal.

name: Dos Pilas
summary: Petexbatún war capital founded by a Tikal splinter dynasty, abandoned amid Late Classic warfare.

name: Aguateca
summary: Fortified Maya centre burned and abandoned so abruptly that whole household assemblages survive in place.

name: Piedras Negras
summary: Usumacinta kingdom whose stela series let Proskouriakoff prove Maya glyphs record real dynastic history.

name: Yaxchilán
summary: Riverbend Maya capital famed for carved lintels showing royal bloodletting and captive-taking.

name: Bonampak
summary: Small Maya court whose unfinished murals give the most vivid surviving images of Maya war and ritual.

name: Palenque
summary: Western Maya capital of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, with the tomb-bearing Temple of the Inscriptions.

name: Toniná
summary: Terraced acropolis city that captured Palenque's king and carries one of the latest Long Count dates.

name: Comalcalco
summary: Westernmost Maya city, built of fired brick because the delta had no stone.

name: Copán
summary: Southeastern Maya capital whose Hieroglyphic Stairway and sculpture record a 16-king dynasty.

name: Quiriguá
summary: Motagua valley city that beheaded Copán's king and raised the tallest stelae in the Maya world.

name: Caracol
summary: Sprawling low-density Maya city of agricultural terraces and causeways that defeated Tikal in 562.

name: Xunantunich
summary: Belize River valley centre that grew as neighbouring Maya capitals collapsed, crowned by El Castillo.

name: Lamanai
summary: One of the longest continuously occupied Maya towns, lasting from the Preclassic into the Spanish mission era.

name: Altun Ha
summary: Coastal Maya trading town whose tomb yielded the great jade head of the sun god K'inich Ahau.

name: Cerros
summary: Late Preclassic Maya coastal trading centre that built early painted temple facades then was abandoned.

name: Cuello
summary: Among the earliest known Maya villages, key evidence for the Preclassic origins of Maya society.

name: Cobá
summary: Northern Maya city of lakes and the longest sacbe causeway network, reaching 100 km to Yaxuná.

name: Dzibilchaltún
summary: Very long-lived Yucatec city with the equinox-aligned Temple of the Seven Dolls and a sacred cenote.

name: Uxmal
summary: Greatest Puuc-style Maya city, with the oval Pyramid of the Magician and elaborate lattice mosaic facades.

name: Kabah
summary: Puuc city linked to Uxmal by causeway, its Codz Poop facade covered in hundreds of rain-god masks.

name: Sayil
summary: Dispersed Puuc garden-city whose household survey reshaped views of Maya urban density.

name: Labná
summary: Puuc town dependent on chultun cisterns, known for its ornate corbelled arch gateway.

name: Edzná
summary: Maya city with a vast hydraulic canal and reservoir system and a five-storey palace-pyramid.

name: Chichén Itzá
summary: Cosmopolitan Terminal Classic capital fusing Maya and central Mexican styles around the Sacred Cenote.

name: Mayapán
summary: Last great walled Maya capital, ruling northern Yucatán by confederacy until factional revolt destroyed it.

name: Tulum
summary: Walled Maya seaport on Caribbean cliffs, a hub of the late canoe trade in salt, obsidian and cotton.

name: Kaminaljuyú
summary: Highland Maya capital controlling El Chayal obsidian, with early monumental sculpture and canal irrigation.

name: Izapa
summary: Pacific piedmont cacao centre whose narrative stelae bridge Olmec and Maya art and calendrics.

name: Takalik Abaj
summary: Pacific slope city with both Olmec-style boulders and early Maya stelae, a cultural transition point.

name: Iximché
summary: Kaqchikel Maya capital on a defensive plateau, briefly the first Spanish capital of Guatemala.

name: Q'umarkaj
summary: K'iche' Maya capital of the Popol Vuh lineages, burned by Pedro de Alvarado in 1524.

name: Zaculeu
summary: Mam Maya highland capital, surrendered after a Spanish siege by starvation in 1525.

name: Joya de Cerén
summary: Maya farming village buried by volcanic ash, preserving ordinary houses and gardens like a New World Pompeii.

name: Chalchuapa
summary: Long-lived southeastern centre on the cacao and obsidian routes, disrupted by the Ilopango eruption.

name: Quelepa
summary: Lenca-area centre east of the Lempa marking the non-Maya southeastern frontier of Mesoamerica.

name: Guayabo de Turrialba
summary: Largest known chiefly centre of Costa Rica, with cobbled causeways, aqueducts and stone mounds.

name: Sitio Conte
summary: Panamanian chiefly burial centre whose gold-rich graves define Coclé elite culture on the isthmus.

name: En Bas Saline
summary: Large Taíno chiefly village on Hispaniola, likely the seat of Guacanagarí who met Columbus in 1492.

name: Caguana
summary: Principal Taíno ceremonial plaza complex with petroglyph-lined bateyes for the ball game.

name: Huaca Prieta
summary: Preceramic Peruvian coastal mound village, among the oldest continuously occupied sites in the Americas.

name: Áspero
summary: Fishing port of the Caral complex with the earliest monumental platform mounds on the Peruvian coast.

name: Caral
summary: Oldest known city in the Americas, with sunken circular plazas and pyramids and no evidence of warfare.

name: Bandurria
summary: Late Archaic coastal centre contemporary with Caral, evidence that early urbanism was regional not singular.

name: Sechín Bajo
summary: Holds one of the oldest monumental plazas in the Americas, a sunken circular court dated near 3500 BCE.

name: Cerro Sechín
summary: Casma valley temple faced with carved warrior and dismemberment reliefs, early monumental violence imagery.

name: El Paraíso
summary: Enormous Late Preceramic stone complex in the Chillón valley, an early experiment in monumental civic space.

name: Kotosh
summary: Highland ritual site whose Temple of the Crossed Hands marks early Andean religious architecture.

name: La Galgada
summary: Preceramic highland temple complex of superimposed ritual chambers in the Kotosh tradition.

name: Chankillo
summary: Fortified ceremonial centre with the oldest known solar observatory in the Americas, the Thirteen Towers.

name: Chavín de Huántar
summary: Pilgrimage centre whose underground galleries and Lanzón spread the first pan-Andean religious style.

name: Pukara
summary: First urban centre of the northern Titicaca basin, ancestor of Tiwanaku sculpture and sunken-court design.

name: Chiripa
summary: Early Titicaca village-temple complex with sunken courts that prefigure Tiwanaku's civic form.

name: Huacas de Moche
summary: Capital of the Moche state, dominated by the adobe Huaca del Sol and the mural-covered Huaca de la Luna.

name: Sipán
summary: Moche royal centre whose intact Lord of Sipán tomb transformed understanding of Andean kingship.

name: Pampa Grande
summary: Late Moche capital of nucleated urban compounds, burned and abandoned within two centuries.

name: Galindo
summary: Late Moche walled city marking the shift to defensive, class-segregated urbanism after the coastal collapse.

name: Dos Cabezas
summary: Moche pyramid town known for elite burials of unusually tall men with elaborate copper-gold regalia.

name: Cahuachi
summary: Nasca pilgrimage capital of adobe mounds, a ceremonial city largely empty between festivals.

name: Ventilla
summary: Largest Nasca habitation settlement, the residential counterpart to ceremonial Cahuachi.

name: Tiwanaku
summary: High-altitude Andean capital of the Gateway of the Sun, ruling by colony and cult across the altiplano.

name: Lukurmata
summary: Second city of the Tiwanaku state on Titicaca's shore, centre of raised-field farming.

name: Khonkho Wankane
summary: Pre-Tiwanaku altiplano civic-ceremonial centre with monoliths and sunken courts.

name: Wari
summary: Capital of the first Andean empire, a dense walled city of orthogonal compounds and administrative colonies.

name: Conchopata
summary: Wari secondary city and ceramic workshop centre known for oversized ritual urns and offering smashes.

name: Pikillacta
summary: Vast rigidly planned Wari provincial city near Cusco, apparently abandoned before completion.

name: Viracochapampa
summary: Unfinished Wari administrative city in the northern highlands, a template of imperial planning.

name: Marcahuamachuco
summary: Fortified highland ridge city of great galleries and round halls, independent neighbour of Wari.

name: Batán Grande
summary: Sicán religious and metalworking capital whose tombs and arsenical bronze industry dominated the north coast.

name: Túcume
summary: Late Sicán capital of 26 adobe pyramids around a sacred hill, later absorbed by Chimú and Inca.

name: Chan Chan
summary: Largest adobe city in the world, Chimú capital of ten walled royal ciudadelas and deep sunken wells.

name: Farfán
summary: Chimú provincial administrative centre later reused by the Inca to govern the north coast.

name: Pachacamac
summary: Great oracle city of the central coast, a pilgrimage centre respected by Wari, Ychsma and Inca alike.

name: Cajamarquilla
summary: Large adobe city of the Rímac valley, a major inland urban node beside Pachacamac.

name: La Centinela
summary: Capital of the Chincha kingdom, whose maritime merchants traded by balsa raft along the Pacific coast.

name: Kuélap
summary: Chachapoya cloud-forest citadel of hundreds of round houses behind twenty-metre walls.

name: Gran Pajatén
summary: Chachapoya montane centre of round buildings with mosaic stone figures on the eastern Andean slope.

name: Cusco
summary: Inca imperial capital and ritual navel of Tawantinsuyu, laid out with ceque lines and Sacsayhuamán above.

name: Sacsayhuamán
summary: Monumental Inca ceremonial fortress above Cusco, built of megalithic interlocking stonework.

name: Machu Picchu
summary: Inca royal estate and ritual retreat on a granite ridge, abandoned soon after the Spanish conquest.

name: Ollantaytambo
summary: Inca planned town still lived in on its original grid, with terraced temple works and a 1537 battle site.

name: Pisac
summary: Inca royal estate guarding the Sacred Valley entrance, with terraces, sun temple and cliff tombs.

name: Choquequirao
summary: Remote Inca ceremonial complex with llama mosaics in its terraces, a refuge in the Vilcabamba resistance.

name: Vitcos
summary: Capital of the neo-Inca state of Vilcabamba, with the oracle rock of Ñusta Hispana nearby.

name: Huánuco Pampa
summary: Purpose-built Inca provincial capital with 500 storehouses and a vast plaza for state hospitality.

name: Vilcashuamán
summary: Inca administrative city with a stepped ushnu platform where the emperor sat to review the province.

name: Tambo Colorado
summary: Well-preserved Inca coastal administrative centre built in painted adobe rather than stone.

name: Raqchi
summary: Inca way-station city on the Collasuyu road, dominated by the great Temple of Wiracocha.

name: Tomebamba
summary: Northern Inca capital and Huayna Capac's birth city, wrecked in the civil war before the Spanish arrived.

name: Ingapirca
summary: Cañari centre rebuilt as Ecuador's principal Inca complex around an elliptical sun temple.

name: Quito
summary: Northern highland centre that became an Inca administrative seat and Atahualpa's base in the civil war.

name: Tumbes
summary: Inca frontier port and temple town, the first Andean city Pizarro saw and the gateway to the conquest.

name: Cajamarca
summary: Inca provincial city with baths and plaza where Atahualpa was seized in November 1532.

name: El Fuerte de Samaipata
summary: Carved sandstone ritual rock and settlement on the Inca eastern frontier facing the Chiriguano lowlands.

name: Incallajta
summary: Largest Inca site east of the Andes, a frontier garrison city with a vast kallanka great hall.

name: Aldea de Tulor
summary: Oldest known village of the Atacama oases, clustered circular adobe rooms buried by desert sand.

name: Quilmes
summary: Largest pre-Columbian settlement in Argentina, a Calchaquí stone hill city that resisted Spain for decades.

name: El Shincal de Quimivil
summary: Southern Inca provincial capital of Kollasuyu, with paired ceremonial hills flanking a great plaza.

name: Ciudad Perdida
modern_name: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia
summary: Tairona stone-terraced city in the Sierra Nevada, hub of a network of some 200 linked settlements.

name: Pueblito
summary: Tairona coastal town of stone terraces and staircases, abandoned under Spanish pressure.

name: Hunza
summary: Seat of the Zaque, northern ruler of the Muisca confederation of the Colombian highlands.

name: Bacatá
summary: Capital of the Zipa and largest Muisca centre, a town of cane-and-clay enclosures rather than stone.

name: Sugamuxi
summary: Muisca sacred city whose great Sun Temple was the confederation's chief pilgrimage shrine.

name: San Agustín
summary: Dispersed funerary and ceremonial landscape with the largest group of megalithic statues in South America.

name: Tierradentro
summary: Andean ceremonial zone of painted underground shaft tombs cut into hilltops.

name: Upano Valley complexes
summary: Amazonian garden-city network of platform mounds and sunken roads, revealed by lidar in the Upano valley.

name: Marajó mound complexes
summary: Amazonian chiefdom of artificial habitation mounds and elaborate funerary urns at the mouth of the Amazon.

name: Santarém
summary: Large Tapajó town on terra preta soils at the Tapajós-Amazon junction, described as densely populated in 1542.

name: Kuhikugu
summary: Cluster of plaza towns joined by roads and moats, evidence of garden urbanism in the southern Amazon.

name: Llanos de Mojos earthworks
summary: Casarabe low-density urban network of causeways, canals and stepped mound centres on seasonal floodplain.

name: Acre geoglyphs
summary: Hundreds of geometric ditched enclosures in western Amazonia, ceremonial not defensive, cut into managed forest.

name: Watson Brake
summary: Oldest known mound complex in North America, eleven mounds raised by hunter-gatherers with no agriculture.

name: Poverty Point
summary: Vast concentric-ridge earthwork centre and long-distance exchange hub built by non-farming societies.

name: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks
summary: Geometric earthwork complexes of the Scioto valley, ritual gathering places for a continental exchange network.

name: Newark Earthworks
summary: Largest geometric earthwork complex on Earth, aligned to the 18.6-year lunar standstill cycle.

name: Fort Ancient
summary: Hopewell hilltop enclosure of 5.7 km of embankment walls with solar and lunar gateway alignments.

name: Cahokia
summary: Largest city north of Mexico, Mississippian capital of 120 mounds around Monks Mound and a grand plaza.

name: East St. Louis Mound Center
summary: Second largest mound precinct of greater Cahokia, a burned and abandoned satellite city.

name: Moundville
summary: Mississippian political and religious capital of 29 mounds on the Black Warrior River, later a necropolis.

name: Etowah
summary: Fortified Mississippian town whose marble effigy statues and copper plates define the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex.

name: Spiro Mounds
summary: Western Mississippian gateway centre whose Craig Mound held an unmatched trove of shell, copper and textiles.

name: Ocmulgee
summary: Early Mississippian town with a reconstructed earth lodge council chamber, ancestral to Muscogee history.

name: Aztalan
summary: Palisaded northern outpost of Mississippian culture, far up the Rock River from Cahokia.

name: Angel Mounds
summary: Palisaded Mississippian town on the Ohio River, a regional capital of the middle Ohio valley.

name: Kincaid Mounds
summary: Major Mississippian centre of the lower Ohio, key to the concept of a Cahokia-linked political sphere.

name: Toltec Mounds
summary: Plum Bayou culture mound and embankment centre laid out on solar alignments, pre-dating Mississippian towns.

name: Winterville
summary: Mississippian mound capital of the Yazoo basin, a ceremonial centre with few permanent residents.

name: Emerald Mound
summary: Second largest earthwork platform in the United States, ceremonial centre of the ancestral Natchez.

name: Town Creek
summary: Pee Dee culture palisaded ceremonial town on the Mississippian northeastern edge.

name: Crystal River
summary: Long-lived Gulf coast mound and stelae complex, a burial and trade centre of Woodland Florida.

name: Mount Royal
summary: St. Johns River mound town with a long causeway to a pond, linked by trade to distant Mississippian centres.

name: Chaco Canyon
summary: Ancestral Pueblo ceremonial and political core of great houses, great kivas and straight roads across the desert.

name: Aztec Ruins
summary: Planned great house on the Animas River, a successor centre after Chaco's decline.

name: Salmon Ruins
summary: Chacoan outlier great house on the San Juan, later reoccupied by Mesa Verde communities.

name: Mesa Verde
summary: Ancestral Pueblo cliff-dwelling towns of the Mesa Verde plateau, depopulated within a generation after 1280.

name: Yellow Jacket Pueblo
summary: Largest known Ancestral Pueblo village in the Mesa Verde region, with over a hundred kivas.

name: Canyon de Chelly
summary: Continuously inhabited canyon of Ancestral Pueblo cliff villages, later a Navajo heartland.

name: Wupatki
summary: Multi-storey pueblo built after the Sunset Crater eruption, where Pueblo, Sinagua and Hohokam traits met.

name: Betatakin and Keet Seel
summary: Short-lived Kayenta cliff villages abandoned wholesale during the late 13th-century migrations.

name: Snaketown
summary: Principal Hohokam town, with ballcourts and the canal irrigation that made the Sonoran desert farmable.

name: Pueblo Grande
summary: Hohokam platform-mound town controlling the largest canal system in the prehistoric Americas.

name: Casa Grande
summary: Classic Hohokam great house of caliche walls with astronomical apertures, abandoned by about 1450.

name: Paquimé
summary: Adobe city linking the Southwest and Mesoamerica, with macaw pens, ballcourts and piped water.

name: La Quemada
summary: Fortified hilltop city on Mesoamerica's northern frontier, with causeways and a hall of columns.

name: Guachimontones
summary: Teuchitlán capital of unique concentric circular pyramid complexes in western Mexico.

name: Acoma Pueblo
summary: Mesa-top pueblo among the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in North America.

name: Taos Pueblo
summary: Multi-storey adobe pueblo lived in for a millennium, a northern Rio Grande trade hub with the Plains.

name: Oraibi
summary: Hopi mesa village, one of the oldest continuously occupied settlements in the United States.

name: Hawikuh
summary: Largest Zuni town, mistaken for a city of gold by Coronado's expedition in 1540.

name: Pecos Pueblo
summary: Fortified frontier pueblo controlling trade between the Rio Grande farmers and Plains bison hunters.

name: Paako
summary: Tiwa pueblo of the Sandia foothills, abandoned during the colonial disruptions of the 17th century.

name: Huff Village
summary: Fortified Mandan earthlodge town on the Missouri, an early plains village-urban form.

name: Double Ditch Village
summary: Large Mandan earthlodge town with successive defensive ditches, depopulated by smallpox.

name: Ozette
summary: Makah whaling town whose mudslide-buried plank houses preserved an entire Northwest Coast village.

name: SGang Gwaay
summary: Haida plank-house town with standing mortuary poles, emblem of Northwest Coast village urbanism.

name: Cathlapotle
summary: Chinookan plankhouse town on the lower Columbia, a hub of the Northwest riverine trade.

name: Talepakemalai
summary: Earliest well-documented Lapita stilt-house village, starting point of the Pacific settlement expansion.

name: Teouma
summary: Oldest Lapita cemetery in the Pacific, the founding population evidence for Remote Oceania.

name: Bourewa
summary: Earliest known settlement in Fiji, the Lapita beachhead for colonising the central Pacific.

name: Nukuleka
summary: Founding Lapita village of Tonga, the first human settlement in Polynesia proper.

name: Mulifanua
summary: Only known Lapita site in Samoa, now submerged, marking the eastern limit of the first Polynesian push.

name: Mangaasi
summary: Long-occupied post-Lapita village that gave its name to a distinct central Vanuatu ceramic tradition.

name: Chief Roi Mata's Domain
summary: Residence, cave and mass burial island of a paramount chief whose peace-making order survives in oral tradition.

name: Mu'a
summary: Capital of the Tu'i Tonga maritime chiefdom, with terraced langi tombs of dressed coral slabs.

name: Heketā and Haʻamonga ʻa Maui
summary: Earlier Tu'i Tonga seat with a coral trilithon gateway, abandoned when the court moved to Mu'a.

name: Pulemelei
summary: Largest ancient structure in Polynesia's west, a stepped stone platform at the heart of a settlement complex.

name: Nan Madol
summary: Saudeleur capital of nearly 100 artificial islets built of basalt logs, a ceremonial city on a reef lagoon.

name: Leluh
summary: Walled basalt city of chiefly compounds and canal streets, Kosrae's counterpart to Nan Madol.

name: House of Taga
summary: Chamorro latte-stone village whose megalithic pillar houses defined Mariana settlement architecture.

name: Gachpar
summary: High-ranking Yapese village of stone platforms, paths and rai stone money, head of a tributary network.

name: Badrulchau
summary: Monolith and terrace complex of Palau's earthwork era, evidence of large organised pre-contact settlement.

name: Taputapuātea
summary: Central marae of the Polynesian world and node of the Oro cult, from which voyages and lineages radiated.

name: Rapa Nui
summary: Island society of dispersed hamlets and ahu platforms that carved and moved nearly a thousand moai.

name: Orongo
summary: Ceremonial village of stone-slab houses on a crater rim, used seasonally for the birdman competition.

name: Wailua
summary: Royal seat of Kaua'i, a sacred river district chaining heiau, birthstones and a place of refuge.

name: Hōnaunau
summary: Chiefly compound and walled place of refuge where kapu-breakers were granted sanctuary.

name: Kahikinui
summary: Dryland Hawaiian settlement district of hundreds of house sites and shrines, a study in intensive rain-fed farming.

name: Kohala field system settlements
summary: Dense coastal-to-upland Hawaiian villages tied to a vast walled dryland field system supporting chiefdoms.

name: Taipivai
summary: Marquesan valley polity of stone paepae platforms and tohua plazas with monumental tiki.

name: Meʻae Iipona
summary: Marquesan ceremonial site with the largest stone tiki in Polynesia outside Rapa Nui.

name: Ara Metua settlements
summary: Ring-road and marae network organising Rarotonga's districts, a rare paved road system in Polynesia.

name: Maungakiekie
summary: Largest Māori pā, a terraced volcanic cone fortress-town holding several thousand people.

name: Wairau Bar
summary: Earliest substantial settlement in New Zealand, a founding East Polynesian village and burial ground.

name: Kohika
summary: Waterlogged Māori lake village whose preserved wooden houses and canoes document pre-contact life.

name: Budj Bim
summary: Gunditjmara aquaculture landscape of eel channels, weirs and stone house clusters, a sedentary Aboriginal settlement.

name: Brewarrina fish traps
summary: Vast stone fish-trap complex on the Barwon that hosted large intertribal gatherings and shared harvests.

name: Lake Mungo
contested: Included as a long-term occupation and ritual landscape, not a city.
summary: Ancient lakeside occupation and burial landscape with the earliest known cremation, a deep-time Aboriginal settlement.

name: Kuk Swamp
summary: Independent centre of agricultural origins, with drained garden mounds supporting dense highland populations.

name: Palembang
summary: Riverine capital of Srivijaya, the thalassocracy that controlled the Malacca and Sunda straits.

name: Muara Jambi
summary: Largest Buddhist temple-city complex in Sumatra, a monastic and trading centre of the Malayu polity.

name: Trowulan
summary: Brick city of canals and reservoirs that served as capital of the Majapahit maritime empire.

name: Prambanan
summary: Royal temple-city of Hindu Mataram on the Kewu plain, abandoned when the court moved east.

name: Temasek
summary: Fortified 14th-century port settlement on Fort Canning hill, precursor to modern Singapore.

name: Kota Batu
summary: Early Bruneian capital and China-trade port on Borneo's north coast, forerunner of the sultanate.

name: Butuan
summary: Balangay-building trading polity of northern Mindanao with early gold work and Song-era China links.

name: Tondo
summary: Pasig delta trading polity named in the 900 CE Laguna Copperplate, later the core of Manila.

name: Sugbu
summary: Visayan port polity and regional entrepôt where Magellan's expedition landed in 1521.

name: Pejeng
summary: Capital district of early Balinese kingdoms, with rock-cut sanctuaries and the great Moon of Pejeng drum.
